Adopt pytest as the Python test framework: it discovers, runs, and reports tests from the command line, lets you signal failure with a plain assert statement, works for unit through system/functional levels, and can even run existing unittest or nose suites.

Install and run pytest inside a per-project virtual environment; because pytest is versioned separately from the interpreter you can run the latest pytest against legacy Pythons, and on Windows activate the environment with venv\Scripts\activate.bat.
Follow pytest's naming conventions so tests are auto-discovered: name files test_<x>.py or <x>_test.py, functions and methods test_<x>, and classes Test<X>.

Read pytest outcomes correctly and preserve the ERROR-vs-FAIL distinction: outcomes are PASSED, FAILED, SKIPPED, xfail, XPASS, and ERROR, where ERROR marks a failure outside the test body (in a fixture or hook).
Understand that every pytest test runs in three phases — setup, call, teardown — with setup and teardown supplied by fixtures.

Write assertions as a plain 'assert <expression>' and rely on pytest's assert rewriting for detailed failure diagnostics (exact failing line and value diff); add -v to see the full diff when output is truncated.

Test for expected exceptions with 'with pytest.raises(ExpectedException):' (the test fails if no or a different exception is raised) and capture the exception via 'as excinfo' to assert on its message or args.
Declare a fixture with @pytest.fixture(); a test requests it by naming it as a parameter and pytest runs it before the test, and a fixture may both do work and return data.

Assert on warnings issued by code under test with the recwarn fixture (a list of warnings exposing category/message/filename/lineno; recwarn.clear() to reset) or the equivalent pytest.warns() context manager.

Package a pytest plugin as a minimal module plus setup.py, registered via the setuptools entry_points 'pytest11' group, implementing behaviour through hook functions (e.g. pytest_addoption, pytest_report_header, pytest_report_teststatus); include the required setup fields, use py_modules (or packages for multiple modules), and provide a README.

Test plugins like any other code using the bundled pytester plugin: enable it (pytest_plugins='pytester'), generate example tests with testdir.makepyfile, run them via testdir.runpytest, and assert on result.stdout.fnmatch_lines and result.ret (0 pass / 1 fail); follow the make-example, run, examine-output, check-exit-code pattern, keep each test checking one thing, and install the plugin before running its tests.

Measure code coverage with coverage.py via the pytest-cov plugin (pytest --cov=<src>, --cov-report=html for line detail), but treat 100% coverage as a heuristic rather than a goal — untested code may indicate a missing test or dead code, and coverage does not replace thinking.

Choose mock tooling and strategy deliberately: monkeypatch plus the mock package (unittest.mock since Python 3.3, with pytest-mock as a convenient interface) cover test-double needs; because mock-based tests are white-box, decide up front what to mock and where — for example test functionality at the API layer and mock that layer when testing the CLI.

Reach for the right execution plugin per need: pytest-repeat (--count) to reproduce flaky failures, pytest-xdist (-n) to parallelize independent tests (with overhead, so not a linear speedup, and run sequentially when a resource is single-access), and pytest-timeout to bound tests that may hang.

Reach for the right reporting or analysis plugin per need: pytest-instafail and pytest-sugar for live failure output, pytest-html for filterable session reports, and static-analysis plugins (pytest-pycodestyle/--pep8, pytest-flake8/--flake8, flake8-docstrings) to surface style and lint failures as test failures.

Use framework-specific plugins for web testing (pytest-selenium, pytest-django which replaces Django's unittest-based support, pytest-flask), and share your own code with the built-in packaging tools (a pip-installable project via a minimal setup.py, a source distribution, and a wheel) rather than emailing zipped directories.
Prefer plain test functions over class-based tests for simple modules and when starting out, since pytest does not require class inheritance.
Prefer pytest's single plain 'assert' with its rich data-structure diffs over unittest's many specialised assertion methods; use -v/-vv to reveal a withheld diff.
Adopt pytest incrementally on legacy suites: it runs existing unittest.TestCase tests unchanged, so migration needs no rewrite.
In xunit-style pytest tests, use setup_function/teardown_function and reset or delete per-test state so a mutation cannot make a later test pass or fail for the wrong reason.
Measure coverage with pytest-cov as a signal for where tests are missing, not as a mandate for 100%.
Debug with escalating tools: start with print statements, move to pdb.set_trace() when print is insufficient, and use pytest --pdb to break at a test failure.
Use pytest fixtures to inject data and behaviour into tests by declaring the fixture name as an argument; leverage built-in fixtures (monkeypatch, capsys, tmpdir).
Test Jupyter notebooks as part of the suite with the pytest nbval plugin (which executes every cell), but be cautious with output-checking mode when cells produce nondeterministic or image output.

Select and scope test runs precisely: rely on implicit recursive discovery, or pass explicit files/directories, a file::test node id, a -k name expression, and preview a selection with --collect-only before running.
Tag subsets of tests with custom markers (@pytest.mark.<name>) and select them with -m marker expressions (which support and/or/not) so related tests run together even across files.
Build runnable subsets such as smoke tests with markers: a test may carry many markers and a marker may tag many tests, and marked tests are selectable together (even across files) with -m.
Run any subset by directory, file, class, method, node id, name expression, or marker, and run pytest -v to discover the exact node-id syntax for a specific target.

Parametrize a test with @pytest.mark.parametrize(argnames, argvalues) to run it against many data sets (each reported separately, and applicable to a class); make case identifiers readable with the ids parameter or pytest.param(id=...), and quote a node id containing spaces, brackets, or parentheses when rerunning one case.

Parametrize fixtures to multiply coverage: @pytest.fixture(params=[...]) runs every dependent test once per value (read via request.param), ids gives readable identifiers, and isolating an environment/backend choice in one parametrized fixture (e.g. ['tiny','mongo']) runs the whole suite against each option — remembering that fixture parametrization multiplies all dependent tests while test parametrization multiplies only that test.

Migrate a legacy unittest suite incrementally under pytest: pytest runs unittest tests and both styles in one session, pytest markers can be applied to unittest tests, and rewriting to fixtures shrinks the files; watch for session-scope resource conflicts between a unittest tearDownModule and a pytest session fixture, resolving them by sharing the pytest session fixture on the TestCase via @pytest.mark.usefixtures (needed only for shared session-scope resources).

Follow pytest's discovery conventions: a plural 'tests' directory, 'test_' file prefix, 'test' function/method prefix, 'Test' class prefix, and no __init__ on test classes — otherwise tests are silently skipped.
Control failure handling and iteration speed with run-control options: -x and --maxfail to stop early, and --lf/--ff to rerun or prioritize previously failed tests.
Tune output verbosity and traceback detail to the task with -v/-q, --tb=<style> (including --tb=no/line), -l for locals, -s to surface prints, and --durations to find the slowest tests.

Customize pytest locally through conftest.py and ini files, introspect with -h/--markers/--fixtures, and remember that the available options, markers, and fixtures depend on the target path because conftest.py files are loaded along it.

Use pytest.ini for project-wide configuration (at most one) and conftest.py as a local plugin for hooks and fixtures; put hooks/fixtures shared across subdirectories in tests/conftest.py, adding per-subdirectory conftest.py files as needed.

Organize and share fixtures with conftest.py: pytest resolves a requested fixture by name first in the test module then in conftest.py; a lower-level conftest.py serves its directory and subdirectories; never import conftest.py, since pytest loads it automatically as a local plugin.

Activate fixtures appropriately: request by parameter when you need the return value, use @pytest.mark.usefixtures for classes when you do not (it gives no return value), and reserve autouse=True for always-run code whose data tests do not depend on — otherwise prefer named fixtures; rename with name= for clarity.

Use pytest's builtin fixtures for common needs (temporary files, CLI options, cross-session cache, output capture, environment variables, warnings); reusing common fixtures is valuable enough that pytest bundles them.

Add and read custom command-line options via pytestconfig: register options with the pytest_addoption hook (only in a plugin or the top-level conftest.py, never a test subdirectory) and read them with pytestconfig.getoption; pytestconfig (a shortcut to request.config) can also be requested from other fixtures.

Recognize that a top-level conftest.py is already a local plugin: find third-party plugins on PyPI, the pytest docs, and pytest-dev on GitHub, install with pip (pin with ==, install offline via --find-links, or from a Git repo), and prototype a hook-based behaviour change in conftest.py before packaging it.

Store pytest configuration in pytest.ini, tox.ini, or setup.cfg (the format is largely the same) and enable xfail_strict; override discovery with python_files/python_classes/python_functions only for a strong reason such as migrating a large existing suite, doing so gradually by listing both old and new patterns.

pytest supports xUnit-style setup/teardown fixtures at module, function, class, and method level (setup_module/teardown_module, setup_function/teardown_function, setup_class/teardown_class, setup_method/teardown_method), whose module/function/cls/method parameters are optional convention.

Prefer normal pytest fixtures over xUnit fixtures and avoid mixing the two: xUnit fixtures do not appear in --setup-show/--setup-plan, have no session scope (module is widest), apply to every test in a class regardless of need, nest at most three levels, cannot be parametrized, and can only be optimized by grouping tests.
Direct most testing at the interface just below the user interface (the API / subcutaneous layer) rather than at the final end-user interface.
Keep test code in a directory separate from the package source (tests/ vs src/) as a best practice.

Make the package under test importable by installing it locally with pip (which needs a setup.py); use editable mode (pip install -e .) when you want to keep changing its source while it stays installed.

Separate functional tests from unit tests by directory so a subset can be run easily and failure signals stay meaningful: functional tests should break only on intentional functionality changes, while unit tests may break during refactoring.
Organize Selenium functional tests with unittest.TestCase-style classes, descriptive test method names, framework assertions, and setUp/tearDown browser lifecycle management.
Mirror the source layout in the tests directory and separate distinct test types (unit vs functional) into sub-directories so tests are easy to locate and run.
Use object-oriented, class-based structure only where the paradigm fits; prefer a functional style for many unit tests.
Cover a module with both isolated unit tests and end-to-end functional tests, and in class-based tests initialise shared state in setUp and release it in tearDown for clean, independent runs.

Manage tests you should not run normally with the builtin skip/skipif/xfail markers: skip unconditionally, skipif on a Python expression (reason required), and xfail to run-but-expect-failure; set xfail_strict so an unexpected pass fails, always give a reason, and surface reasons with -rs.

Use fixtures rather than old xUnit setup/teardown for setup, teardown, and test data: in a yield fixture the code before yield is setup and after yield is teardown, and autouse=True applies it without being named.

Treat fixtures as the separation of 'get ready' (setup) and 'clean up' (teardown) from tests: in a yield fixture the teardown after the yield is guaranteed to run, and fixtures can be consumed by tests or composed by other fixtures.

Push as much setup (the GIVEN) into fixtures as possible so a FAIL means the behaviour under test broke: an error inside a fixture is reported as ERROR rather than FAIL, so keeping setup in fixtures preserves that distinction; add GIVEN/WHEN/THEN comments when the test's intent is not obvious.

Trace and introspect fixtures while developing them: use --setup-show to see setup/teardown order (F=function, S=session scope) and --fixtures to list the fixtures available to a test and where each is defined.

Choose fixture scope deliberately: the scope parameter (function/class/module/session, default function) is fixed at the fixture's definition and sets setup/teardown frequency; a fixture may depend only on same-or-wider-scoped fixtures; do expensive setup once at session scope and reset state per test with a small function-scoped fixture.
Verify production-like logging by provoking an error under DEBUG=False, ensuring tracebacks reach standard output, and restoring broken test fixtures afterward.

Use tmpdir for a per-test, auto-cleaned temporary directory (a py.path.local — wrap in str() for a path string); because it is function-scoped, use tmpdir_factory (with .mktemp) for class/module/session scope; pytest keeps only the most recent temp base directories, and --basetemp overrides the location.

Create wider-scoped temporary directories by writing your own fixture (of the needed scope) that uses tmpdir_factory, and build a shared temporary data file once in a wider-scope fixture rather than recreating it per test.

Keep tests independent and order-independent so any test can run in any order with repeatable results; when you deliberately need cross-session state use the cache fixture (cache.get/set, keys namespaced with '/', JSON-serializable values), inspect or reset it with --cache-show/--cache-clear, and reach request.config.cache from any scope.
Identify tests robustly with request.node.nodeid (which works even for parametrized tests), sanitizing characters such as colons when using it in filenames or cache keys.

Capture and assert on stdout/stderr with the capsys fixture (out, err = capsys.readouterr(), which returns output since the function start or last call) and use capsys.disabled() to let specific output bypass capture.

Use monkeypatch to modify environment variables, attributes, and dictionary items for a test's duration with automatic undo: setenv/setattr/setitem and their del forms, syspath_prepend to shadow a module, chdir for cwd-dependent code, and the raising parameter; combine with unittest.mock for mock objects.
Use monkeypatch's self-cleaning helpers (setattr/delattr, setitem/delitem, setenv/delenv, syspath_prepend, chdir) so patched state is restored after each test.

Never let a side-effecting function touch the real environment (for example the user's home-directory file); redirect it to a temporary location, and prefer patching the specific function a module calls over a broad, OS-dependent environment variable.

Test docstring examples with doctest: run them via --doctest-modules (each code-bearing docstring is a separate test) and inject shared symbols with the doctest_namespace fixture in an autouse top-level conftest.py so the docstrings stay uncluttered.
Embed runnable examples as doctests in docstrings so documentation doubles as executable, coverage-counted tests.

Distribute a plugin by building a source distribution (python setup.py sdist) and installing it from a shared directory (upgrade with --upgrade); scaffold new distributable plugins with cookiecutter-pytest-plugin.
Grow pytest plugins from simple functions into a packaged plugin only once functionality expands or multiple projects can reuse it.

Prevent duplicate-filename collisions by placing an __init__.py in every test subdirectory (without them, cross-directory runs fail collection with an 'import file mismatch' error); add these files habitually rather than waiting for a collision.

Debug failures efficiently: drop into pdb at the failure point with --pdb, combine it with --lf -x (and -l/-v/--tb) to jump to and inspect the first previously failed test, and use pdb commands such as p/pp, l, a, u/d, and q.
Use mocks (test doubles) to swap out parts of the system and isolate the code under test.
Use the reserved setup/teardown (and setupclass/teardownclass) methods to provide shared state and to clean up artifacts so tests do not pollute each other.

Bake standing options and marker discipline into configuration: use addopts to always apply chosen options and --strict to require that every marker be declared (in the markers section), which catches marker typos.

Test packages across multiple environments with tox: install and run it (it builds a source distribution, creates a virtualenv per target environment, installs dependencies, runs the suite, and prints a per-environment summary); adopt it whenever the package must run in multiple environments.

Integrate pytest with CI (e.g. Jenkins) that runs the suite after each commit: emit results with --junit-xml (the only flag required; --junit-prefix and junit_suite_name refine naming), run inside a virtual environment installing the project first, keep build logic in a version-controlled script, and cover multiple environments via separate jobs or by calling tox.
Use tox to run the test suite across multiple Python versions via a tox.ini with an envlist and a [testenv] section defining deps and commands.
Drive behavior with test-first, outside-in TDD: write an expected-failing test, make the smallest code change that moves the failure forward, and repeat until the user-level behavior passes.
While learning rigorous TDD, write tests for even simple behavior so tests are already present when complexity grows.
Use functional tests for user-visible behavior and wiring confidence, and unit tests for implementation details, edge cases, and clean internal behavior.
Write functional tests as readable user stories, using comments for intent and context rather than restating mechanics that should be clear from the code.
For behavior-preserving redesigns, keep the old functional test as a regression test while a new functional test proves the new multi-user behavior and URL shape.
Keep commits small and reviewable: inspect status and diffs, separate substantial functional-test specification changes from implementation, and commit at coherent tested milestones.
Refactor only under passing-test protection, without mixing in new behavior, and commit the completed structural change as its own milestone.
Debug browser tests with clear durable assertions and temporary inspection aids, replacing arbitrary waits with robust wait helpers when available.
Use explicit Selenium polling waits that retry lookup and assertion failures, re-raise the final failure on timeout, and avoid premature generalization.
Keep unit tests focused on logic, flow, configuration, and template selection; leave mostly constant HTML appearance to browser-level checks and templates.
Change broad designs through controlled working-state-to-working-state steps, using the current expected failure to choose one narrow next move and avoiding speculative features.
Test layout and styling with minimal browser smoke checks that prove CSS-driven behavior works without freezing the visual design.
For production static files, collect app assets into STATIC_ROOT, keep generated copies out of version control, configure a production serving strategy, and verify it with layout functional tests.
Serve app static files through Django’s static URL prefix and use StaticLiveServerTestCase for functional tests that depend on staticfiles support.
Reduce deployment risk by running functional tests against container and staging environments, rerunning them after each fixed deployment layer because the next layer may fail independently.
Automate deployment steps that affect correctness, while separating server provisioning from application deployment and keeping staging close enough to production to be meaningful.
Commit the Dockerfile only after functional tests pass against the container with the intended ports, mounts, and runtime configuration.
Productionize incrementally: start from a crude green container, then change one production concern at a time while functional tests guard behavior.
When external-server tests cannot connect, use inline TEST_SERVER targeting plus layered diagnostics such as server output, curl, docker exec, docker ps, and docker inspect.
Keep runtime database state outside the container image; attach persistent storage and run migrations against the deployed runtime database.
Drive environment-specific settings from runtime configuration, keeping secrets out of source and using persistent per-environment secret storage appropriate to deployment maturity.
Ship a useful early version to learn from users, but treat deployment as a risk area covering networking, dependencies, database state, static files, and security settings.
Write infrastructure automation declaratively and idempotently so repeated runs converge on the desired state for fresh and partially configured servers.
For dynamic resource URLs, capture typed URL parameters, accept them in the view, and use them to select only the requested resource data.
Use REST-inspired URL design pragmatically: GET resource pages, POST action endpoints, and resource URLs that reflect the data model without overfitting strict API rules.
For POST endpoints that create or update list resources, add route and view behavior under tests that separately check persistence and redirects to the relevant resource URL.
Keep unit tests focused on one concern, splitting save behavior from response behavior and using assertRedirects for redirect-after-POST checks.

For Django model changes, declare persistent fields and relationships explicitly, generate migrations carefully, avoid rewriting used migrations, and update legacy creation paths that violate new constraints.
Prefer the smallest useful product slice that can teach whether the application idea works.
Set up each project in an isolated virtual environment with the expected Python, Django, Selenium, browser, and IDE interpreter configuration before running project work.
Keep commands and paths anchored to the project directory that contains manage.py, and initialize Django so manage.py lands in that directory.
Put the project under version control as soon as the first tested setup exists, and ignore generated or local-state files such as databases, virtualenvs, bytecode, and caches.
Isolate each project's Python interpreter and dependencies in a virtual environment (or container), and install packages with pip only inside it — never into the system interpreter.
Treat Django or Selenium import failures as environment problems first: verify the virtual environment, working directory, and active Python before debugging application code.
Use an explicit failing placeholder to mark the unfinished point in a functional test and interpret reaching it as progress through earlier behavior.
When unsure what to do next, rerun the relevant tests and let the current failure define the next task.
Write one behaviour per test with a descriptive name, and avoid bundling many unrelated assertions, so a failure message alone pinpoints the broken expectation.
Choose the testing framework pragmatically: use Django-compatible unittest tooling early and defer more complex live-server tooling until the workflow needs it.
Use the Django test client and Django assertion helpers to test URL routing and response behavior through more of the Django stack, then remove redundant lower-level direct-call tests.
Keep ORM-learning tests distinct from ideal production model tests, recognizing database-backed Django tests as integrated lower-level checks.
Do not let tests interfere through persistent state; use Django-managed live-server tests or equivalent isolation instead of manual database cleanup.
Run LiveServerTestCase-based functional tests through Django discovery, keep them in a separate package when workflows cross app boundaries, and use live_server_url instead of fixed localhost.
Use Django template inheritance to remove shared boilerplate after comparing templates, defining blocks for variable regions, and rerunning functional tests after the refactor.
When a test behaves unexpectedly, re-check the intended goal, edited file, user behavior, command, and traceback before changing application code.
Before trusting a new automated test location, add a deliberate failing smoke test to prove the runner discovers it.
In Selenium tests, choose element lookup APIs according to intent: singular lookup for required elements, plural lookup for collections, and keyboard APIs for user-like input.
Move nontrivial HTML into Django templates and render them with Django render rather than building HTML in Python strings.
Pass dynamic values to Django templates through render context dictionaries and test that the intended template path is still used.
For POST forms in Django, include CSRF support and unit-test POST handling with Django’s test client data dictionaries.
Use triangulation deliberately: a crude implementation may pass briefly, but add another test when the current tests allow unacceptable cheating.
Test GET and POST paths separately when a view handles both, and safely handle missing POST fields on non-POST requests.
Apply DRY cautiously in tests: tolerate early duplication, but refactor repeated patterns after the third similar occurrence.
Extract repeated data into setup and repeated behaviour into non-test helper methods, and refactor/regroup test classes that grow too complex.
Introduce database persistence through Django models when behavior must remember multiple submitted items across requests.
Run the test subset that matches the current loop: fast app unit tests for implementation work, functional tests after unit-level green, and both when uncertain.
Keep Selenium, browser, and browser-driver versions aligned when browser tests begin failing or hanging for environmental reasons.
When one browser session represents multiple users, delete cookies between users and document that test mechanic with meta-comments separate from the user story.
Treat trailing slashes and form action URLs as part of the tested contract because small mismatches can break routing after navigation changes.
After a URL refactor passes, intentionally perturbing a route can confirm that tests would catch a broken mapping.
Introduce new URLs incrementally: point them at existing behavior first when possible, then split views, tests, and templates as responsibilities become distinct.
After a responsibility moves to a new page or view, simplify the old template/view and remove tests for behavior that no longer belongs there.
Model parent-child persistence with a ForeignKey and tests that save the parent, assign children to it, and verify the persisted relationship.
Use targeted anti-hack fixtures, such as an extra parent object, when they prevent plausible incorrect implementations without trying to test every impossible mistake.
Pass the current resource object to templates that need to build resource-specific URLs, and assert that context contract directly when it matters.
Before a structural URL refactor, commit a passing state; then move app-specific routes into app urls.py, include them with a prefix, and alias top-level view imports.
Remove unused Django apps from production configuration when they add unnecessary static output or deployment surface.
Do not use Django runserver for production; use a production WSGI server such as Gunicorn and address production ports and core Django settings.
It is acceptable to recreate a local development database during early migration churn only when it has no important data; do not carry that habit into production.
Move production app source into a src directory once deployment work introduces project-level files outside the runtime application tree.
Write down and run a deployment workflow manually before automating it, and store the pipeline/deploy definition as a checked-in config file versioned with the source.
Start Docker work with a minimal verified Docker setup and a first Dockerfile that chooses a Python base image, copies source, sets WORKDIR, and defines the default command.
Install dependencies inside the image, preferably in an image-local virtual environment on PATH, and use rebuild-and-run loops plus Docker process commands to test and control each Dockerfile change.
When platform-specific deployment debugging stalls, search exact error messages after narrowing the problem with local checks.
Disable DEBUG in production and keep SECRET_KEY out of source code because debug pages and checked-in secrets expose sensitive data.
Manage runtime dependencies with a pinned requirements file copied into the Docker build before source, excluding test-only dependencies from production installs.
Declare dependencies in requirements.txt and, for deployable projects, pin them by freezing installed versions; pin test tooling into the environment for reproducibility.
Treat running containers as non-root as a production security improvement even if the book leaves the exact implementation unfinished.
Production readiness requires a production server, static-file strategy, safe settings, usable logs, and one-at-a-time configuration changes guarded by frequent tests.
Operate public servers with SSH access, sudo-capable non-root users, DNS A records for hostnames, and explicit awareness that server security needs further study.
Verify and debug remote containers over SSH with docker ps and docker logs, treating logs as the first diagnostic source when startup fails.
Automate image transfer in the playbook: build locally when needed, handle target architecture, export or registry-transfer the image, upload or pull it, and load it on the server.
Publishing a container is required for external access; map the server’s normal HTTP port to the app’s container port for a standard web URL.
Maintain an automated regression test suite for any project expected to change or grow, so that no change can silently break existing behaviour.
Treat testing as the foundation of automation and run tests plus quality reports on every check-in to source control.
Treat writing tests as design pressure: if code is hard to test, refactor it to be more granular and modular rather than leaving it fragile.
Treat hard-to-test or heavily-patched code as a design smell signalling insufficient modularity, and design new code for testability from the start.
Recognise that without tests you cannot know software works, and that writing tests before or during implementation shapes code toward modular, maintainable structure.

Control complexity as the essence of development: keep each method's cyclomatic complexity below ~10, since higher complexity correlates strongly with faults and is nearly impossible to cover with tests.
Replace manual terminal/REPL verification with fast automated tests, because manual checking does not scale past a flag or two and is error-prone.
Put every project under version control (git) as a non-negotiable baseline of professional practice.
Scaffold projects for quality from the start with a standard structure: a version-controlled repo, a CI config, a .gitignore, a README, a Makefile and a tests directory.
Adopt a repeatable naming/location convention for virtual environments (e.g. ~/.<reponame>) to remove per-project decisions and clutter.
Standardise routine project tasks behind a Makefile (setup, install, test, lint, all) so every project is built, tested and linted the same way.
Prefer conventions over ad-hoc choices, because they compress complex tasks into memorable steps and cut error rates.
On macOS, install the project's Python via Homebrew rather than the system Python.
Configure the editor/IDE to use the interpreter from the project's activated virtual environment so linting and test runs target the right environment.
Make the lint step complete and authoritative, covering all relevant code (Python and, where present, the Dockerfile) rather than a partial subset.
Be a pragmatic minimalist about testing: some testing is proper and none is foolish, but strict 100% coverage / full TDD is often not worth the ROI — avoid zealotry that is unsustainable.
Tune test verbosity to context: verbose (-vv) on the build server or when drilling into a failure, normal locally.
Make a linter a mandatory part of the process and fail the build on code that cannot execute; checking in non-executable code is never acceptable.

Generally disallow linter errors in source, while allowing rare, documented exceptions (e.g. false positives from external libraries), and configure the linter to the project rather than accepting defaults blindly.
Introduce pylint to an existing codebase gradually by first disabling the refactor and convention categories (--disable=R,C) to focus on real errors.
Adopt an opinionated auto-formatter (e.g. black) to remove style debates and silence formatting complaints.
Keep unit tests contained and reproducible by substituting fakes/fixtures for external services rather than making real calls.
Have fixtures return factory closures so tests construct objects at test time, and give new fixture/fake parameters defaults so existing tests are not disrupted.
Reach for monkeypatching only when a dependency with the desired behaviour cannot be passed in as an argument.
Stub a dependency globally with an autouse fixture in conftest.py that uses monkeypatch, when it must be replaced across the whole session.
When patching, target the name where it is used, not where it is defined, using monkeypatch.setattr (string path or module+attribute).
Cap the number of patches per test at roughly three; beyond that, refactor rather than accumulate brittle patches.
For large, hard-to-test code, extract the specific functionality you need into a smaller testable unit rather than patching around a huge function.

Prefer dependency injection over patching: allow dependencies to be passed as arguments defaulting to the real one (e.g. def main(argv=None): argv = argv or sys.argv), so tests inject fakes with no patching.
Never patch built-in modules such as os; inject the dependency or wrap the built-in call in a small function instead.
Test across multiple Python versions even within Python 3, because subtle behavioural changes surface bugs; never assume dict insertion order on interpreters older than 3.7.
Express multidimensional tox matrices compactly with factors (curly-brace expansion), remembering that dashes separate factors, and constrain the envlist to only the intended version/branch pairs.
Pin tool versions per tox environment using factor-specific deps or a dedicated [testenv:<name>] override when a dependency has dropped support for an older Python.
Extend tox beyond unit tests to run linting, docs and other validations; when building docs in CI, treat warnings as errors (sphinx-build -W) so warnings fail the build.
Distinguish Continuous Integration (automated build+test on every change) from Continuous Delivery (also deploying to a new environment) when designing a pipeline.
Drive local and build-server workflows through the same commands (e.g. a Makefile), and run tests, linting and formatting locally so they pass before pushing.

Represent infrastructure as checked-in code (IaC) so environments can be provisioned and deployments automated with humans out of the loop; treat automated test + delivery as a requirement for modern systems.
Do not commit generated build artifacts to source control; ignore them and provide a clean target to remove them.
Sanity-check downloaded tool binaries (e.g. run --version) and pin explicit tool versions in the pipeline rather than always pulling latest, to keep builds reproducible.
Trigger builds via a source-control webhook so every push runs the pipeline, and deploy with a sync-and-prune command so the target matches the freshly built output.
Test command-line tools with their runner (e.g. click.testing.CliRunner), asserting the process exit status and the textual output separately.
Add functional and health-check tests that exercise real end-to-end workflows, because they surface pathological behaviour that unit tests miss.
Never silently swallow all exceptions and exit with status 0; log errors instead, as hidden failures are the worst debugging anti-pattern.
Rescue a legacy mess in order: establish a lint baseline, extract nested logic into tested functions, add logging, and use the debugger only as a last resort.
Decompose logic into small, single-purpose, documented methods so the same behaviour becomes testable and readable instead of a monolithic function.
Avoid technical zealotry when debugging: there is no perfect methodology, so investigate empirically and take nothing for granted.

Define 'clean code' operationally by metrics — close to 100% test coverage, cyclomatic complexity under 10 for all classes/methods, and a near-10 pylint score — and design software to run under automated tests from the start.
Use static-analysis tools (complexity, duplication, general quality) to measure quality objectively rather than by eye, and scope coverage reporting to the module/package under test.

Remember that neither testing nor static analysis is a panacea: the goal is not merely to solve the problem but to build software you can prove works, so resist needless complexity and over-confident design.
Write a README that explains how to build and use the project, and surface a CI build-status badge so build health is visible.
Apply the same automated-quality discipline (build systems, static analysis, repeatable processes) to data-science and notebook code as to traditional software.
